# Faheem Ahmed

> Faheem Ahmed (known as "The Pharmacy Guy") is a UK-based educator, author and
> consultant working across healthcare and education. He provides teaching,
> training and consultancy for clinicians, teams and organisations, and
> publishes books and clinical writing.

## What he offers
- Teaching: CPD and diploma programmes, OSCE and exam preparation, lectures and webinars.
- Training: prescribing and clinical pathways, healthcare team upskilling, placement and supervision support.
- Consultancy: clinical service and clinic design, governance and compliance, growth and positioning.

## Authority
- Educator and trainer across healthcare and education.
- Author of clinical and professional books and writing.
- Consultant on healthcare services and ventures.
- Creator of clinical content as The Pharmacy Guy.

## Key topics
Healthcare education, clinical training, independent prescribing, professional
development, medicine, dentistry, clinical governance, healthcare consultancy.

## Writing
Practical articles and guides on independent prescribing, healthcare education and clinical practice.
- Get on Your ICB's Prescribing List (Before the Deadline) — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/get-on-your-icb-prescribing-list/ — Faheem's time-sensitive call to action for pharmacy owners in England: NHS independent prescribing in community pharmacy is OPT-IN, and the ICB will not come and find you. On 31 July 2026 NHS England published a professional assurance framework and wrote to every Integrated Care Board (ICB) — with around £51,000 each — telling them to build a process to identify, approve and onboard prescribing pharmacies, in place by August 2026, and to onboard the pharmacies that have EXPRESSED AN INTEREST. Onboarding runs from a list; no name on it = not in the queue. The key trap: in many areas the thing you must complete is labelled a "readiness survey", which sounds optional but IS how you express interest — it maps which pharmacies have Independent Prescribers (IPs) and DPPs and can meet the bar, to inform commissioning. Don't wait for a separate official form. Eligibility bar: a minimum 24 hours/week of prescriber availability, prescription management to national guidance, and ICB governance met — and because Pharmacy First and contraception are face-to-face, read the 24 hours as prescriber time in the building (a single locum IP one afternoon a week won't clear it; national eligibility detail still being finalised). Deadlines are set locally and vary by ICB: as an example, Thames Valley opened its survey on 21 August 2026 and closes it Sunday 6 September 2026. What's actually unlocked for 2026/27: prescribing within the existing contract — Pharmacy First + Contraception, up to five new prescriber-only minor-ailment pathways being considered from autumn, plus prescription management — i.e. Pharmacy First with a prescription pad instead of a PGD, not a licence to prescribe anything. What to do today: go to your LPC website, search "prescribing"/"readiness survey", check you can offer 24 hrs/week and name which IPs cover which site, submit one entry per pharmacy; no form there → email your LPC chief officer. It's not just the form: delivering needs policies/procedures, monthly clinical supervision with a named mentor, an annual prescribing appraisal and a prescribing portfolio. No IP / not prescribing / stuck finding a DPP = the real bottleneck to fix first. Educational commentary, not legal/regulatory advice; the 6 September date is Thames Valley-specific — verify your own deadline with your LPC, ICB and NHS England. Companion to Faheem's video on the ICB prescribing deadline; links to his prescribing-governance and DPP articles. Sources: NHS England professional assurance framework (31 July 2026); CPE Prescribing within the CPCF.
- How Do You Prove You're Competent? (And Why Pharmacists Get Struck Off) — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/how-to-prove-you-are-competent/ — Faheem's argument that clinical competence is evidenced, not conferred: a certificate proves you attended and passed at a point in time, but the regulator judges what you actually do. Anchored on Epstein & Hundert's definition (competence is the habitual and judicious use of knowledge, skills, reasoning, values and reflection in daily practice) plus Miller's pyramid (knows → knows how → shows how → does; certificates test the bottom, regulators judge "does") and Benner's novice-to-expert path (competence grows through experience, it isn't a badge handed over). Scope of practice is the line you must not cross — it's personal to you and about evidenced competence, not qualifications on the wall; prescribing outside it is a fast route to fitness-to-practise action. Prompted by a real 2025 case in which a pharmacist was suspended for prescribing irrationally and unsafely, outside their competence — qualifications were no defence because the GPhC regulates practice, not certificates. How to prove competence in three steps: (1) a course for knowledge (Level 7 for prescribing-level work — necessary but not sufficient); (2) a portfolio to evidence applied practice — a defined scope, self-assessment against the RPS prescribing competency framework, real anonymised cases, reflection, audit, feedback and supervision (your "does", written down); (3) formal RPS credentialing where it exists, as an independent external marker rather than self-claim. Educational commentary and personal opinion, not legal/regulatory advice; the 2025 suspension is illustrative, not about a named individual. Companion to Faheem's video on why pharmacists get struck off. MEDLRN provides Level 7 learning, portfolio support and scope-of-practice help.
- Creating a Niche Pharmacy Business: Why Niche Gets Bought — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/creating-a-niche-pharmacy-business/ — Faheem's case for building a specialist rather than generic pharmacy, prompted by a niche pharmacy business that recently changed hands for around £2.1m (an illustrative market example, not a valuation of any specific business). The core thesis: generic community pharmacy competes on price and volume — capped NHS reimbursement, squeezed margin, easy to replicate on the next high street, so hard to sell for a premium — whereas a niche pharmacy "gets bought" because it builds things that are hard to copy. A niche (weight management, dermatology, menopause/women's health, men's health, mental health/ADHD, travel health, or medical cannabis) builds four assets: a defined patient base that returns (recurring revenue), a private-prescribing income stream not capped like the NHS contract, a brand a buyer can keep trading under, and genuine expertise. How to pick a lane: find the overlap of real private-pay demand, your own clinical credibility, and a viable income model; pick one and go deep before adding a second. Going niche doesn't mean abandoning NHS dispensing — keep it as a stable floor and build the niche as the growth engine on top. The part people get wrong: governance IS the value. Marketing brings patients in, but what makes the business sellable is governance a buyer can trust — clean records, right registrations, proper prescribing frameworks, clinicians within scope, no compliance skeletons. A niche with weak compliance is a liability, not an asset, so compliance isn't overhead — it's what you're building to sell. Educational commentary and personal views, not legal/financial/regulatory advice. Links to Faheem's articles on private-clinic compliance and prescribing governance. Faheem helps owners choose a lane, stand up the service and build the governance that turns an idea into a sellable asset.
- The Governance Behind Community Pharmacy Prescribing: NHS England's 2026 Rulebook, Explained — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/community-pharmacy-prescribing-governance/ — A plain-English explainer of the governance package NHS England published on 31 July 2026 for independent prescribing in the national community pharmacy services (Pharmacy First, Contraception, Prescription Management) from autumn 2026. Why it exists: from summer 2026 every new MPharm graduate registers as an independent prescriber, but pharmacists have no NHS performers list (unlike GPs, dentists, optometrists), leaving a gap between fitness to practise (the GPhC's remit — skills, knowledge, health, character) and fitness for purpose (safe and competent to deliver THIS service, in THIS setting, under THIS contract) — you can be fit to practise yet not fit for purpose. The package plugs that gap across three layers. Layer 1, the individual prescriber: an annual fitness-for-purpose declaration of prescribing scope of practice (submitted to the employer, updated when scope changes — the annotation says you CAN prescribe, the declaration says what you WILL); regular clinical supervision with a named supervisor/prescribing mentor (monthly is the example); an annual prescribing appraisal (additional to, not the same as, GPhC revalidation); a portfolio evidencing prescribing decisions including decisions NOT to prescribe, errors, audits, reflections; annual self-assessment against the RPS/Royal College of Pharmacy Prescribing Competency Framework; Level 3 safeguarding (most sit at Level 2 — a real gap); and indemnity that specifically covers prescribing. Layer 2, the employer/contractor: the checks (registration, enhanced DBS within 3 years, right to work, English language, HPAN check, two structured references, training evidence, indemnity), record-keeping for at least 5 years, supporting supervision/appraisal/induction, not pushing scope expansion without risk assessment, and a concern-escalation ladder (local support → ICB clinical leadership → NHS Resolution) that can end in asking the ICB to remove the prescriber from the NHSBSA prescriber dataset — switching off NHS prescribing (a fitness-for-purpose action that does NOT touch GPhC registration). Layer 3, the ICB/commissioner: an EPS cost centre per contractor with each prescriber assigned by registration number so every item is tracked via ePACT2 (scope, formulary, high-risk meds, antibiotics, controlled drugs, volumes, costs, outcomes, referrals); conflict-of-interest management (remuneration rewards quality of decisions and outcomes, NOT prescription volume); digital/clinical safety requirements (DCB0129/0160, EPS by default, records access via NCRS/GP Connect, same/next-day GP communication, DSPT Standards Met, CIS2/AAL3 identity); ~£51,000 per ICB for 2026/27 readiness; and onboarding targets to 31 March 2027 — because ICBs control onboarding, compliance is the ticket to play. What's unlocked: prescribing within the existing Pharmacy First seven conditions and contraception (using clinical judgement to complete the episode of care rather than referring back for being just outside a PGD), prescription management (e.g. an alternative when an item is out of stock), and up to five new prescriber-only pathways being considered (pending clinical reference group sign-off). Most of the framework is "should" (best practice) not "must" (statute), but onboarding makes compliance effectively mandatory. Educational summary of NHS England guidance, not legal/regulatory advice; verify with NHS England, your ICB and the GPhC. Companion to Faheem's video series on prescribing governance (part one: the professional assurance framework).
- How to Make Your Private Prescribing Clinic Safe and Compliant (When No One Regulates It) — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/how-to-make-your-private-clinic-compliant/ — The practical follow-up to the regulatory-loophole article: given that a solo pharmacist-led private clinic can fall between the GPhC (which regulates pharmacies) and the CQC (which doesn't regulate pharmacists), what should an independent prescriber actually put in place before an inspection? Faheem's checklist: (1) training and certification, in place, current and evidenced; (2) proper insurance/indemnity, watertight for the activities offered; (3) adopt the nearest standards even though they don't strictly bind you — the GPhC standards for pharmacies and the CQC best-practice standards — and implement both, because in an inspection the first question is always "what rules, policies and procedures were you following?"; (4) build a governance structure so you are not the sole decision-maker — e.g. non-executive directors (a pharmacist, a doctor, a nurse, someone outside the profession) through whom questions and decisions pass, which makes your judgement defensible; (5) written policies and procedures, regular audits and reflection on practice; (6) documentation as the thread through all of it — the evidence that everything actually happened. Underlying it all is trust, without which a business is hard to run. The mindset: behave as though you are regulated, because if something goes wrong you will be judged as though you were — and the individual pharmacist is always answerable to the GPhC (fitness to practise). Educational commentary, not legal/regulatory advice; verify CQC/GPhC requirements for your specific service. Companion to Faheem's TikTok video "Pharmacist ran clinic — no CQC or GPhC regulation, what do you do?". MEDLRN runs GPhC & CQC compliance courses and is developing a compliance tool.
- The Regulatory Loophole for Pharmacists: Who Regulates a Private Prescribing Clinic? — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/the-regulatory-loophole-for-pharmacists/ — Faheem Ahmed explains a genuine regulatory gap around pharmacist-led private prescribing clinics. An independent prescriber pharmacist can open a private prescribing clinic almost anywhere and prescribe on private prescriptions. The question is who regulates that business: the CQC regulates clinics and professions such as doctors and nurses; the GPhC regulates pharmacies and pharmacists; but a solo pharmacist running a private prescribing service (no doctors or nurses involved, and not a registered pharmacy) can fall into the gap between the two, so the business itself may have no clear regulatory oversight — that is the loophole. It is not UK-wide: Wales and Scotland have addressed it because they recognised it was happening, while in England (at the time of writing) the loophole is still open. The crucial caveat: the gap is in the business, not in you — the individual pharmacist remains regulated by the GPhC, which can still investigate and raise fitness to practise, and many pharmacists have got into trouble for not following good practice. Whatever the premises, you must work to good practice, the GPhC Standards for Pharmacy Professionals, and (when prescribing) the RPS Prescribing Competency Framework; that is what protects your registration, not the regulatory status of the building. Practical takeaway: do not build a clinic on a loophole — set it up properly (scope, governance, documentation, indemnity, the right registrations), because you carry the responsibility and the direction of travel is towards closing these gaps. Educational commentary, not legal/regulatory advice; requirements are nuanced, vary by nation and change — verify with the CQC and GPhC. Companion to Faheem's TikTok video "The regulatory loophole for pharmacists". MEDLRN runs GPhC & CQC compliance courses to help set up private clinics properly.
- What First-Time Buyers Should Understand Before Acquiring a Pharmacy — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/what-first-time-pharmacy-buyers-should-know/ — Faheem Ahmed's frank checklist of what to understand before buying your first pharmacy — and, he stresses, before buying any business. Four things. (1) The business model: really understand how you are paid, especially the average item value (roughly the average NHS reimbursement per dispensed item), because NHS income is volume x that value; he cites a colleague who bought a pharmacy without grasping this and found stock of ~£50,000 but NHS income of only ~£20,000 because the average item value had fallen to about £4 — you cannot see the risk you are taking on until you understand how the money actually comes in, so know that, not just turnover. (2) Compliance is TWO regimes, not one: most buyers think only of the GPhC and forget compliance with the NHS contract, but both carry obligations and both affect value and risk. (3) HR and TUPE: you inherit the existing staff with their rights protected under TUPE, so you cannot simply install your own team or dismiss people — a colleague who tried ended up at employment tribunals. (4) Accounting: understand basic accounting and bookkeeping, and beware tax, where first-time owners repeatedly get stung. The bigger point: model, compliance, people, books is the homework before buying any business; pharmacy just adds NHS payment mechanics, dual compliance, TUPE-protected teams and dispensing-tax quirks. Educational only, not financial/legal/tax advice; figures illustrative. Companion to Faheem's video "What a first-time buyer should understand before acquiring a pharmacy". MEDLRN runs GPhC & CQC compliance and NHS-contract courses for buyers who want to build these skills.
- Training Pharmacy Technicians: Why Remote Supervision Is Coming — and What It Means for Pharmacists — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/training-pharmacy-technicians/ — Faheem Ahmed's frank commentary, prompted by a reported ~£360,000 tender to deliver clinical-skills training for pharmacy technicians in London (tied to Pharmacy First; Chemist+Druggist, 3 Aug 2026). His read: that contract is a signal of direction, and within five years — or less — remote supervision is coming to community pharmacy. The likely shape is a return to something like the old superintendent model, but at scale: one pharmacist overseeing multiple shops and delegating day-to-day responsibility to technicians trained up to Level 4. The message to pharmacists is not to panic but to move — those who keep only dispensing and never develop toward prescribing or regularly upskill will struggle, while those who upskill will have a bigger role, not a smaller one. He draws the parallel with doctors: policy shifted so pharmacist and nurse prescribers took on work GPs used to hold, and the GP job market is tougher for it (practices taking on pharmacist prescribers partly for financial reasons). The role is changing, supervision is going remote, and the winners are the ones who adapt. Opinion/prediction, not settled policy — remote-supervision rules and timelines are evolving, so check current GPhC guidance. Companion to Faheem's TikTok and YouTube video "Training pharmacy technicians — remote supervision is coming".
- How to Set Up a Chain of Pharmacies on Under £200k: Buy the Contract, Not the Shop — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/how-to-set-up-a-chain-of-pharmacies/ — Faheem Ahmed answers a viewer's question: how do independents buy one pharmacy and quickly build a whole chain? The honest answer is that you cannot BUY a chain for under £200k (one decent shop is £500k-plus) — but you can CONTROL one, because the real asset you are acquiring is the NHS contract: a stable, government-backed, bankable income stream. The centrepiece is the "trick" of invoice discounting: your NHS payment statement is guaranteed income (say ~£100k a month), and an invoice-discounting firm will advance cash against it (e.g. two months' ~£200k of income fronted as ~£160k now, minus their drawdown and fee), which you then use as the deposit for the next pharmacy — and repeat, exactly like flipping property. Supporting plays: buying distressed/motivated-seller contracts cheaply, seller financing and deferred consideration, sweat-equity partnerships (you operate, an investor funds), operating before you own, and cutting the cost base while layering private services on the NHS base. It is candid about the danger: you are carrying interest and debt, the T&Cs and hold-backs eat into every advance, and the guaranteed NHS income that makes the statement lendable is exactly what you are mortgaging — leverage cuts both ways. Educational opinion, not financial or legal advice. Companion to Faheem's TikTok video "A chain of pharmacies for £200k — the trick explained".
- Community Pharmacy Independent Prescribing: Is It Worth It? — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/community-pharmacy-independent-prescribing/ — A frank, honest look at what independent prescribing in community pharmacy actually means in practice. Wales and Scotland already let community pharmacists prescribe more broadly, while England is starting much smaller — a new NHS pharmacy prescribing service from around August covering only about five defined conditions, not open or unrestricted prescribing. The piece is candid about the risks: prescribing adds clinical and medico-legal responsibility, and the liability stays with you — the prescriber owns the decision, the assessment and the consequences, regardless of protocols or employer. It also examines the money honestly: being a prescriber does not automatically transform your wage, and whether it is worth it depends on your setting, your appetite for that responsibility and how the service is actually funded and used. Companion to Faheem's video "Community pharmacy independent prescribing — is it worth it?".
- How to Market Your Pharmacy or Clinic in the UK: Authority, Not Just Advertising — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/how-to-market-your-pharmacy-and-clinic/ — A guide to marketing a pharmacy or clinic the durable way, built on the distinction between advertising (paying to interrupt people and push a message) and marketing (building trust, relationships and reputation so patients come to you). The core strategy is to become an authority in your niche rather than the cheapest option: teach, explain and demonstrate expertise so you are the obvious, trusted choice — a position no discount can buy. Practical tactics include using AI to build content at scale (articles, scripts, social posts, email) so a small team can publish consistently, and running free local webinars and talks that educate your community, generate goodwill and bring in patients through value rather than hard sell. It also flags the key legal constraint: the MHRA rule that prescription-only medicines cannot be advertised to the public, so your marketing must promote the service, the clinic and your expertise — not name or picture the POM to pull people in. Companion to Faheem's video "How to market your pharmacy or clinic".
- How to Set Up an Online Prescribing Service in the UK: Governance, SOPs and Safe Prescribing — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/how-to-set-up-an-online-prescribing-service/ — A frank, practical guide to setting up a safe online prescribing service in the UK (pharmacy, clinic or private prescriber). The central message: governance is where clinics fail, not clinical knowledge. The HSSIB (Health Services Safety Investigations Body) is investigating online prescribing and has flagged serious issues, so regulators and insurers now expect real governance, not templates. Core components: an independent governance committee (no shareholders or directors on it — ideally a doctor, a pharmacist, perhaps an ex-inspector and a lay member) that reviews decisions roughly every 6–8 weeks, which is some of the best money a service can spend; bespoke, evidence-based SOPs (standard operating procedures) that reflect what you actually do, backed by regular audits; appropriately trained staff with CVs and references on file; and proper insurance/indemnity. Service-specific safeguards matter — for weight loss, independently verify weight and BMI rather than taking the patient's word; ensure continuity of care and access to the patient's medical records; and never prescribe on a questionnaire alone. Regulation check: confirm whether your model needs CQC registration and that every clinician works within their scope. Educational commentary, not regulatory advice — verify current CQC/GPhC/MHRA guidance before launching. Includes CTAs to MedLrn (training and policies), mentoring, and Clinickly (governance/SOPs and MDT). Companion to Faheem's video "How to set up a safe online prescribing service".
- Should You Pay for a DPP? Who Should Really Foot the Bill — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/should-you-pay-for-a-dpp/ — Faheem Ahmed's opinion piece on whether trainee prescribers should pay for a Designated Prescribing Practitioner (DPP). The principle: paying for a genuine service is convention (universities, pharmacists, taxi drivers are all paid), so a DPP who properly assesses and mentors you — understanding the assessments required and how to assess you against the competency framework — should, by convention, be paid. But the real question is who should pay: the individual, or the state. Faheem's clear view is that the state should reimburse DPPs, because training the next generation of prescribers is a public good; this already happens in Wales (reimbursement on the order of £3,000–£4,000) and some English Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) are reportedly considering it, though it is not universal. A DPP should be reimbursed for the actual work of assessing and mentoring, not merely for holding the title. Timing note: pharmacists qualifying from 2026 register as independent prescribers at the point of registration and don't need a separate DPP — it's the earlier cohort who need one, which is why funding matters most for them. If you must pay, pay for it done properly (real assessment, mentoring, a support network) because "buy cheap, buy twice", and reframe it as investing in education rather than the newest phone. If struggling to find a DPP: start with friends, family and colleagues, use LinkedIn, and if still stuck, organised support like MEDLRN can help (there is a fee; use funding if available). Educational opinion, not regulatory/financial advice; funding rules differ across the UK and change. Companion to Faheem's video "Should you pay for a DPP?". See also the how-to-find-a-dpp-2026 guide.
- The Weight-Loss Pill Is Here — So Why Is Mounjaro Still Better? — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/weight-loss-pill-vs-mounjaro/ — A clinician's plain-English take on the arrival of the first oral GLP-1 weight-loss pill, orforglipron (brand name Foundayo), which was approved in the US in 2026 as a once-daily tablet with no food or water restrictions — and why, despite that, the injection Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is still more effective. The chemistry recap: peptide GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide, and the GLP-1 part of tirzepatide) must be injected because gut proteases (peptidases) and blood DPP-4 cut peptide bonds, destroying an oral peptide; orforglipron is a non-peptide small molecule with no peptide bonds, so it survives the gut and is absorbed intact with no fasting window (deeper build-up in the companion article "Orforglipron explained"). The core argument is single- vs dual-agonist: orforglipron activates only the GLP-1 receptor, whereas tirzepatide is a dual agonist that activates both GLP-1 and GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, another incretin). The added GIP action appears to boost appetite control and fat/lipid metabolism — partly via effects on glucagon and lipolysis (fat breakdown), though the precise mechanism is still debated — so the dual-agonist injection has generally produced greater average weight loss (a cross-trial pattern, not a head-to-head). Why the pill still matters: many patients won't inject, so a needle-free, food-flexible tablet widens who will start and stay on treatment, and is likely to drive another demand boom. Whichever is used, the medicine is a tool not a cure and works best with diet, exercise and resistance training (to protect muscle while losing fat). Educational only, not medical advice or an advert for a POM; orforglipron is US-approved but not yet a routine MHRA-approved UK medicine. Includes a CTA for clinicians wanting to develop weight-loss prescribing skills and a mention of Faheem's ADHD webinar. Companion to Faheem's video on the oral weight-loss tablet.
- Why I Don't Read the Accounts When I Buy a Pharmacy (and What I Verify Instead) — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/why-i-dont-read-pharmacy-accounts/ — Faheem Ahmed's approach to pharmacy due diligence, with a deliberately provocative but precise claim: he doesn't rely on a target pharmacy's prepared accounts, because they are written from information the seller provides and are usually not independently audited or verified, so the headline figures can be "window-dressed". The mechanism to understand is accrual versus cash accounting: under accrual accounting revenue is recorded when invoiced, not when cash is received, so a business can raise invoices and book them as profit without ever receiving the money — and the debtor book can be adjusted to inflate profit — meaning recorded profit is not the same as cash in the bank. Instead he anchors on numbers a third party can confirm: the NHS payment schedules (PPD/NHSBSA schedule of payments) which prove dispensing income, VAT and tax returns submitted to HMRC, PAYE statements which reveal true staffing costs, and the lease, rent, business rates and utility bills; over-the-counter sales he tends to treat as build-able upside as long as NHS income covers the cost base. On the "proper" statements: the balance sheet matters most in a share sale (you buy the company and inherit its current assets, current and long-term liabilities) and far less in an asset sale; reserves can mislead because accumulated reserves may already be spent, so look at what's actually in the bank; and the profit-and-loss account, while useful, is dressable and should never be the thing you buy on. The rule: never buy on the bottom line — verify the income and fixed costs, and treat everything unverified as a claim. Educational only, not financial/accounting/legal advice. Companion to Faheem's video "Why I don't read the accounts when I buy a pharmacy".
- Opening vs Buying a Pharmacy: Which Should You Do? — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/open-or-buy-a-pharmacy/ — A frank, owner's guide to deciding between buying an existing community pharmacy and opening a new one from scratch. What you are really buying either way is the NHS contract — a stable, government-backed income stream that holds its value because it is regular, protected and can be very profitable (fixtures, fittings and stock have value too, but the contract is the prize). There are only two routes to a contract: buy an existing pharmacy that already holds it, or apply for a brand-new one. Most people buy because the business is already set up and running (staff, stock, goodwill, income from day one) and they avoid the brutal grind of starting from scratch (Faheem started one from scratch — a 100-hour-a-week, 8am-to-midnight journey); but a profitable shop doing ~£10k/month profit typically costs £800,000+ (good pharmacies £500k+), and you inherit liabilities and relationships — staff, stock, GP surgeries and patients — that you cannot simply change. Opening from scratch costs far less up front (a ~£750 application) but is controlled market entry: you need local ICB approval, decided on the Pharmaceutical Needs Assessment (PNA, refreshed every 3–5 years), and it typically takes 6–8 months (sometimes up to two years) with red tape and no guarantee. The old trigger of opening next to a new GP practice has largely gone (patients now order medicines remotely), so the situations worth considering now are a new housing estate or a busy parade with genuine unmet need. The decision comes down to your capital, your appetite for risk and grind, and whether you can actually run a pharmacy yourself. Companion to Faheem's video "Should you open or buy a pharmacy?".
- How Does a Pharmacy Make Money? The 4 Income Streams (and Why There Are More) — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/pharmacy-income-streams/ — A frank, owner's guide to how a UK community pharmacy earns, framed as four core income streams with private services on top. (1) NHS dispensing: the core, paying an activity fee of roughly £1.52 per item for 2026/27 (up from ~£1.46) — a thin, largely mechanical and increasingly automated margin that only works at volume (multiply across 10,000–20,000 items/month). (2) NHS services: Pharmacy First for defined minor conditions (UTIs, earache, shingles, insect bites, impetigo) at ~£18 per consultation but largely referral-driven; the contraception service at ~£25 to initiate or continue supply; and the new NHS independent prescribing service in England paying ~£500 setup plus ~£525/month, with a currently narrow list of conditions compared with Scotland and Wales. (3) Over-the-counter retail: a pharmacy is a shop and can sell almost anything (beauty, general sales medicines, everyday goods, even food) — the model Boots and Lloyds built on. (4) Training and education: supervising, teaching and foundation/pre-registration training. The bigger growth comes from private services layered on top — private prescribing, weight loss, ADHD treatment, aesthetics, and GP/dentist/nurse clinics — which is where a pharmacy multiplies rather than just defends its income. Fees are illustrative and move; verify with Community Pharmacy England and the NHS Business Services Authority. Companion to Faheem's video "4 ways a community pharmacy makes money".
- Why You Can't Just Open a Pharmacy (Even If You Have the Money) — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/why-you-cant-just-open-a-pharmacy/ — A plain-English explanation of why you cannot simply open a community pharmacy in England however much money you have, in six stages. (1) It is a controlled market on purpose: NHS funding is finite (a global sum of roughly £3.6bn shared between ~8,000–9,000 pharmacies), so entry is restricted and that scarcity is what gives an NHS contract its value. (2) The gatekeeper is the pharmaceutical list — the register of premises allowed to provide NHS pharmaceutical services; you join it either by a successful new market-entry application or by buying/taking over an existing pharmacy already on it. (3) The rulebook is the NHS 2013 Regs (the NHS (Pharmaceutical and Local Pharmaceutical Services) Regulations 2013), which define market entry through inclusion/exclusion criteria; Health and Wellbeing Boards write the criteria and Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) assess applications. (4) The deciding document is the Pharmaceutical Needs Assessment (PNA), published by each Health and Wellbeing Board roughly every three years, setting out current and future local pharmaceutical need — an application generally succeeds only if it meets a need identified in the PNA, so prospective owners should read their local PNA first; "the existing pharmacy looks busy" is not the test, documented need is. (5) Four application routes: routine (PNA identifies a need), unforeseen (a change since publication, e.g. closures, a new housing estate or GP practice), expected/excepted (change of ownership, consolidation or relocation of existing pharmacies), and now-largely-closed routes (the old 100-hour exemption and distance-selling pharmacies). (6) The process: the application stage typically takes ~30–45 days, but with objections and any appeal (handled by NHS Resolution) the whole thing can take up to six months or more, and can be refused. Practical pointers: application forms come from Primary Care Support England (PCSE), and the NHS pharmacy manual is the companion to the 2013 Regs. Companion to Faheem's TikTok/short video "Why you can't just open a pharmacy — the PNA".
- Critical Thinking in the Age of AI: Why Clinicians Still Need to Think — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/critical-thinking-in-the-age-of-ai/ — A reflective essay (prompted by Faheem's ADHD diagnosis webinar) arguing that AI raises the value of human judgement rather than lowering it. AI has made information abundant and cheap, which makes the scarce, valuable skill judgement — the ability to tell a correct answer from a confident-sounding wrong one. Core arguments: a two-day course (or an instant AI answer) gives you information, not competence, because competence is a state you are assessed into and must maintain, not a certificate earned once; critical thinking matters more in the age of AI, not less, because you can only evaluate an AI answer if you already understand the topic; AI does not reason like a human (it uses a form of logic but lacks human context and accountability), so output quality depends on how you ask and how the tool is trained, and serious domain-trained tools cost real money and effort; knowledge has a shelf life (the webinar psychiatrist would still be using outdated diagnostic criteria had he not kept updating), which is why regulators require revalidation and CPD. Practical guidance for clinicians using AI: treat output as a draft not a verdict, only trust what you can evaluate, check against authoritative sources, never enter identifiable patient data into consumer tools, and keep the accountability for the decision yours.
- 5 Mistakes That Cost Pharmacy Owners Hundreds of Thousands — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/5-mistakes-that-cost-pharmacy-owners/ — Faheem Ahmed's hard-won guide to five avoidable mistakes that cost first-time pharmacy buyers six figures. (1) Overpaying — driven by not knowing how to value a pharmacy, then emotion and bidding wars; a pharmacy worth ~£200k–£300k can attract £700k–£800k offers; value on an EBITDA multiple, set a ceiling and walk away, and beware sellers who take the patient base via a rival online pharmacy. (2) Not understanding NHS payment — the NHS pays in arrears (submit one month, advance the next, balance the month after, so ~90 days behind), and a low average item value bites: one buyer with a ~£4 average item value was paid ~£40k against £80k of stock for 10,000 items. (3) TUPE staff liabilities — you inherit staff and their rights; you cannot simply give notice or rework contracts to remove them, or you face an employment tribunal and thousands in costs (brokers who say otherwise are wrong). (4) Skipping due diligence — understand the process, change-of-ownership and fitness-to-practise checks, and especially stock valuation and contract clauses; one buyer was landed with a £60k unwanted-stock bill and £20k solicitor fees (a straightforward purchase can cost ~£8k or less). (5) The 90-day cash-flow gap — hold working capital and plan a quarter ahead, because a profitable pharmacy can still hit a wall. Companion to Faheem's YouTube video "5 Mistakes That Cost New Pharmacy Owners £100,000s".
- How Much Does a Pharmacy Owner Actually Make? The Honest Numbers — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/how-much-does-a-pharmacy-owner-make/ — A frank, owner's guide to how much a UK community pharmacy actually earns, built around the distinction between turnover, EBITDA and net profit. Turnover is all income coming in (NHS dispensing, private services, retail); EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, which strips out financing and tax variables so lenders and buyers can compare the underlying cash position like-for-like (central to valuing a pharmacy); net profit is what the business keeps after every expense and tax — and none of these equals what the owner personally draws out. As a rough guide, a pharmacy dispensing ~10,000 items/month turns over ~£80k–£100k/month, up to ~£1m/year; net profit on such a business is typically ~10–15% (on the order of £100k/year, ~£8k–£9k/month); and an owner of a single high-volume shop can take home ~£10k/month depending on how they draw it. The bigger money comes from stacking private services (private clinics, weight-loss, online pharmacy, private prescribing, retail) on top of the stable NHS base, or owning several shops you don't work in. Companion to Faheem's YouTube video "How much do pharmacy owners actually make?".
- Should You Buy a Community Pharmacy in 2026? An Honest Look Before You Commit — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/should-you-buy-a-community-pharmacy-2026/ — A frank guide to buying a community pharmacy in the UK in 2026. The cost of entry is six figures (typically £300k–£1m+, with a decent pharmacy usually £500k plus), often funded by savings, a remortgage or loans, so it is a serious commitment and not passive income — it is a hands-on business with staff, admin and red tape. The 2026/27 funding settlement put the global sum at roughly £3.6bn with a ~£340m uplift, but that was largely redistributed (not new) money and only ~10% in nominal terms, down from ~19–20% the year before. Pharmacies relying on the NHS contract alone struggle (reportedly ~78% in year one, ~99% within five years), yet NHS contracts still sell at a profit even when loss-making (e.g. a pharmacy losing ~£100k/year selling for £200k+) because the income stream is stable, government-backed and bankable. Three owner profiles make pharmacy pay: the lean owner-operator (works the hours, minimal overheads, draws profit), the entrepreneur (NHS contract as a stable base plus retail and private services — weight loss, ADHD, online clinic, sub-let rooms, podiatry/beauty), and the cash-rich turnaround buyer (buys distressed cheaply, installs a team, rebuilds, exits up). Companion to Faheem's YouTube video "Should You Open a Pharmacy in 2026? The Honest Truth".
- Faheem Ahmed on GPhC Fitness to Practise: What Really Happens — and 5 Lessons I Learned — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/faheem-ahmed-gphc-fitness-to-practice/ — Faheem Ahmed is open about having been through the General Pharmaceutical Council (GPhC) fitness-to-practise process himself. A plain-English guide to how a fitness-to-practise case works: a concern is raised and investigated, an interim orders committee can impose interim conditions or suspension to protect the public while the facts are established, and an independent Fitness to Practise Committee then decides the case in three stages — findings of fact (on the balance of probabilities), impairment (is fitness to practise currently impaired), and sanction (no action, warning, conditions, suspension or removal). Includes five lessons (understand the process, get specialist legal advice early, be careful what you say, diversify income, build governance) and how to protect your registration in advance with patient-centred standards, training, processes, insurance and an independent governance committee.
- Orforglipron Explained: the Oral GLP-1 Weight-Loss Pill With No Needle — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/orforglipron-explained/ — What orforglipron is (an oral, non-peptide, small-molecule, partial GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes and weight loss), what GLP-1 does (insulin release, glucagon suppression, slowed gastric emptying, appetite suppression), why peptide GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide must be injected (peptide bonds are cut by gut peptidases, and DPP-4 inactivates GLP-1), and why a non-peptide small molecule can be a daily tablet with no fasting window — unlike oral semaglutide, which needs the SNAC absorption enhancer and an empty stomach.
- How to Find a Designated Prescribing Practitioner (DPP) in 2026 — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/how-to-find-a-dpp-2026/ — Why DPPs are scarce in 2026 (pharmacists now qualify as prescribers at registration), who can be a DPP, how to verify eligibility, and a practical step-by-step sequence to secure one.
- Should Pharmacies Dispense at a Loss? Legal vs Moral — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/should-pharmacies-dispense-at-a-loss/ — An argument piece on the economics and ethics of NHS dispensing. Under the NHS pharmacy contract a pharmacy can only refuse to dispense on narrow grounds (unsafe/erroneous prescription, threats of violence, prescriber not legally permitted) — losing money on the item is not one of them. Losses arise because the Drug Tariff (the national reimbursement listing, built from supplier-price research plus an intended margin) updates monthly while market prices move daily; price concessions are meant to bridge the gap but lag badly and have often still paid below cost. Cash-flow compounds it: suppliers are paid day one, while NHS payment runs on a ~3-month cycle (dispense January, claim by 5 February, advance ~10 February, balance in March). The core claim: legal and right are not the same thing (women's suffrage, the Nuremberg laws and same-sex marriage all show law lagging morality), and forcing a private business to subsidise a tax-funded public service from its own pocket is unjust — no other public contract works that way (no construction firm would accept 'it costs you £1m, we pay £500k'). Counter-arguments addressed: 'think of the patients' (collapse serves them worst), 'you signed up to it' (consent doesn't make unjust terms just — like below-minimum-wage contracts; the losses postdate the original contract), and 'if everyone refused the system would collapse' (true — which is an argument for fixing it, not perpetuating it). The fix: make price concessions real-time. Companion to Faheem's YouTube Short "Should pharmacy be dispensing at a loss?".
- How to Demonstrate Clinical Competence (Not Just Credentials) — https://faheemahmed.co.uk/blog/how-to-demonstrate-clinical-competence/ — What clinical competence really means, why a course/title/years of experience don't guarantee it, how to demonstrate and evidence competence (best practice, competency frameworks, mentorship, supervised experience, reflection, support network, portfolio), and how to expand scope of practice safely.
